steps.tx: Skeletal muscle consists of multinucleated cylindrical fibres displaying regular transverse striations under light microscopy. The basic structural and functional repeating unit of a myofibril is the **sarcomere**, delimited between two dark transverse boundary partitions called Z discs (Z lines). Sarcomeres arrange in series along the entire longitudinal length of each myofibril.
steps.say: Skeletal muscle consists of multinucleated fibres displaying cross-striations. The basic contractile unit of a myofibril is the sarcomere, bounded between two dark transverse partitions termed Z discs. Sarcomeres repeat in series along the entire length of the myofibril.

steps.tx: A sarcomere exhibits alternating dark and light bands under polarised light. The dark **A band** is anisotropic, representing the entire longitudinal span of thick myosin filaments with overlapping thin actin filaments at its lateral margins. The width of the A band remains completely constant and unchanging during both muscular contraction and passive stretching.
steps.say: A sarcomere features alternating dark and light bands. The dark A band corresponds to the full length of thick myosin filaments with overlapping actin filaments. The width of the A band remains entirely constant during muscle contraction and relaxation.

steps.tx: The light isotropic band flanking the Z disc is the **I band**, comprising only thin actin filaments without overlapping thick filaments. In the centre of the A band lies a pale region designated the H zone, containing thick myosin filaments alone without thin actin filaments. Bisecting the H zone is the M line, formed by myomesin anchoring adjacent thick filaments.
steps.say: The pale isotropic zone flanking the Z line is the I band, containing only thin actin filaments. In the middle of the A band sits the lighter H zone, housing myosin filaments devoid of actin overlap. Bisecting the H zone is the M line.

steps.tx: Muscular shortening obeys the classic **sliding filament theory**, wherein thin actin filaments slide past thick myosin filaments toward the M line. Cross-bridge cycling between myosin heads and actin draws adjacent Z discs closer together. While individual actin and myosin filament lengths do not change, the I band narrows and the H zone completely disappears.
steps.say: Muscle contraction proceeds via the sliding filament theory, where thin actin filaments slide along thick myosin filaments toward the centre. Myosin cross-bridges pull Z discs closer together. Filament lengths never change, but the I band narrows and the H zone vanishes.

steps.tx: Thin filaments consist of filamentous actin wound with two regulatory proteins: **tropomyosin**, which physically blocks myosin-binding sites on actin during rest, and troponin. Troponin is a heterotrimer: troponin T binds tropomyosin, troponin I inhibits actin-myosin interaction, and troponin C binds calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to trigger the power stroke.
steps.say: Thin filaments comprise actin wound with tropomyosin and troponin. Tropomyosin sterically blocks myosin-binding sites during relaxation. The troponin complex contains troponin T binding tropomyosin, troponin I inhibiting binding, and troponin C binding calcium.

steps.tx: Under the microscope, **cardiac muscle** forms a branching network rather than separate parallel fibres. Each cardiomyocyte carries one central nucleus and joins its neighbours at stepped intercalated discs. Fascia adherens and desmosomes in the transverse steps bear mechanical strain, while gap junctions in the longitudinal steps pass ions quickly, letting atria and ventricles contract as coordinated units.
steps.say: Cardiac muscle consists of branched uninucleated cells connected by intercalated discs. Transverse disc segments transfer mechanical pulling forces, while longitudinal segments carry gap junctions for rapid electrical spread.

vis.alt: Microscopic view of cardiac muscle with branching fibres, single central nuclei and dark intercalated discs joining cardiomyocytes end to end.
vis.caption: Branching cardiac fibres meet at intercalated discs, where desmosomes resist tearing and gap junctions let the electrical signal sweep through the syncytium. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: In contrast to voluntary skeletal muscle, **cardiac muscle** consists of branched uninucleated cardiomyocytes joined end-to-end at specialized junctional complexes termed intercalated discs. Transverse segments of the intercalated disc contain fascia adherens and desmosomes that transmit mechanical tension, while longitudinal lateral segments pack gap junctions that permit rapid electrical syncytial coupling.
steps.say: Cardiac muscle consists of branched uninucleated cells connected by intercalated discs. Transverse disc segments feature fascia adherens and desmosomes to transfer mechanical pulling forces, while longitudinal segments carry gap junctions that enable electrical syncytial activation.

steps.tx: Involuntary non-striated **smooth muscle** lines hollow visceral organs and blood vessel walls, featuring spindle-shaped fusiform cells with a single central elongated nucleus. Lacking sarcomeric organization, smooth muscle cells lack troponin, instead relying upon calcium binding to calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase and phosphorylate myosin heads.
steps.say: Smooth muscle lines visceral organs and vessels, featuring spindle cells with central elongated nuclei. Lacking sarcomeres and striations, smooth muscle lacks troponin, utilizing calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase and trigger contraction.

steps.tx: Thin actin filaments in smooth muscle anchor to proteinaceous structures called **dense bodies** scattered within the sarcoplasm and along the inner sarcolemma. Functionally analogous to Z discs of striated muscle, dense bodies contain alpha-actinin and are interconnected by intermediate filaments (desmin and vimentin), allowing corkscrew contraction of the cell.
steps.say: Thin filaments in smooth muscle anchor to protein dense bodies dispersed through the cytoplasm and membrane. Serving the role of Z discs, dense bodies contain alpha-actinin and anchor desmin filaments, producing a corkscrew twisting contraction.
